#OTD in 1884, Theodore Roosevelt made what he called the best shot he had ever made, paced out the distance to prove it, and kept the bullet.

It had been a miserable day. Up Clear Creek in what is now Wyoming, in country he called "very barren; broken, rolling, treeless, and covered with sage brush." Deep washouts across the road. The wagon stuck three times, and they had to help the team out with ropes hitched to the saddle trees of the riding horses. "Team nearly done out."

Then, in the afternoon:

"Roused three blacktail bucks; shot three times with Winchester at them running, going close but a little high, finally stopping them; two stood side by side; taking careful aim I broke the backs of both with one bullet; distance 431 paces (near 400 yards) actual walking. Best shot I ever made. Kept bullet."

Two deer with one bullet, at a distance he put at close to four hundred yards. It is his own account, in his own diary, and it is the only account we have.

The detail that gives it away is "actual walking." He did not estimate the range. He walked it, counting — 431 paces — because he wanted the number to be right. He knew his own limits. Four years earlier, hunting with his brother Elliott, he had written flatly in the same diary: "Elliott is a good shot; I am not. But I am improving steadily."

So he kept the bullet. Somewhere in the accounting of a life that would include a war, a presidency and a Nobel Prize, a twenty-five-year-old put a piece of lead in his pocket because he wanted to remember.

#OTD in 1897, Assistant Secretary of the Navy Theodore Roosevelt mailed the President of the United States a pamphlet, and quietly told on his own boss in the covering note.

He had spent his "spare hours" that summer assembling every passage he could find in which a previous president had argued for a stronger navy. Washington, Jackson, Lincoln, Grant. Read back to back it struck him as a powerful piece of propaganda, so he decided to publish it. Thomas Jefferson did not make the cut.

Protocol required showing it to his actual superior first. Secretary of the Navy John D. Long — who was already tired of his deputy's loud enthusiasm for battleships — approved it on one condition: that Roosevelt insert the words "in my own opinion" into the introduction, so nobody mistook it for department policy.

Roosevelt agreed, in writing, with every appearance of humility: "Hereafter I shall adopt exactly the rule you suggest about my official publications, and about my general utterances also."

Then he sent an advance copy to President McKinley with a note pointing out this:

"On the first page, where I speak of the need of strengthening the Navy, the words 'in my own opinion,' were put in at the suggestion of the Secretary."

Which is to say: the hedge you are about to read is not mine. It is the Secretary's.

It appeared that year in the Proceedings of the United States Naval Institute, and the Government Printing Office issued it as a pamphlet in September: The Naval Policy of America as Outlined in Messages of the Presidents of the United States from the Beginning to the Present Day. By Edmund Morris's account it drew admiring notice, "timely" being the adjective most often used. Eight months later the United States was at war with Spain, and within weeks the man who compiled it had resigned to go and fight in it.

#OTD in 1910, out of office nearly eighteen months, Theodore Roosevelt spoke to 30,000 people at Osawatomie, Kansas, at the dedication of a park honoring John Brown. Grand Army veterans were in the crowd and he spoke straight at them, quoting Lincoln. What he set out became the manifesto of the Republican insurgency.

By any measure of 1910 it was radical: federal supervision of every corporation doing interstate business, a graduated income tax, an inheritance tax on big fortunes, workmen's compensation, child labor limits. He did not pretend it was small:

"This, I know, implies a policy of a far more active governmental interference with social and economic conditions in this country than we have yet had, but I think we have got to face the fact that such an increase in governmental control is now necessary."

Then he turned on the reformers:

"If I could ask but one thing of my fellow countrymen, my request would be that, whenever they go in for reform, they remember the two sides, and that they always exact justice from one side as much as from the other. I have small use for the public servant who can always see and denounce the corruption of the capitalist, but who cannot persuade himself, especially before election, to say a word about lawless mob-violence. And I have equally small use for the man, be he a judge on the bench or editor of a great paper, or wealthy and influential private citizen, who can see clearly enough and denounce the lawlessness of mob-violence, but whose eyes are closed so that he is blind when the question is one of corruption of business on a gigantic scale."

He knew how he was being read:

"Here in Kansas there is one paper which habitually denounces me as the tool of Wall Street, and at the same time frantically repudiates the statement that I am a Socialist on the ground that that is an unwarranted slander of the Socialists."

The country divided. Some called it socialistic; others, among the greatest speeches ever delivered. Two years later it was the platform he ran on against the man he had put in the White House.

#OTD in 1878, a nineteen-year-old about to start his junior year at Harvard sat down and admitted he had no idea what to do with his life.

"I had a long talk with Uncle Jim about my future life; I have absolutely no idea what I shall do when I leave college."

His father had been dead nearly seven months. Theodore Roosevelt Sr. — the man his son called the best he ever knew — had died in February at forty-six of a malignant tumor of the bowel, after months in which the family watched and could do nothing. The son had not been there at the end.

The next line of the diary is not a plan. It is grief:

"Oh, Father, my Father, no words can tell how I shall miss your counsel and advice!"

And then, immediately, the only thing he can think of to do about it:

"However, for the next two years my duty is clear—to study well and live like a brave Christian gentleman."

That is the whole entry. A boy with no direction, no father, and one rule he has decided to follow until something better arrives.

Uncle Jim was James Alfred Roosevelt, his father's brother, a New York banker, and now the man with the final say over the family's money.

Worth remembering what happens next, and how little of it he could see coming. Within six years he would be a published historian, a state assemblyman, a widower and a rancher. Twenty-three years later he would be president. On this day in 1878 the plan was to study well and behave decently, and that was all of it.

A hundred and twenty-five years ago today, at the Minnesota State Fair, Vice President Theodore Roosevelt quoted the line he is still quoted for.

"A good many of you are probably acquainted with the old proverb: 'Speak softly and carry a big stick—you will go far.'"

Three things about it are not what people assume.

The first is that he had been using it for more than a year and a half, and not about foreign policy. He wrote it down in January 1900, in a letter to Henry Sprague, in a good mood after forcing the New York Republican machine to drop a corrupt state insurance superintendent: "I have always been fond of the West African proverb." The most famous line in the history of American foreign policy started life as a comment on a patronage fight in Albany.

The second is that nobody has found the proverb. No earlier use of it has ever turned up, and Roosevelt never said where he had heard it.

The third is the part that gets left off. The line is not a boast, and the rest of the same paragraph says so:

"If a man continually blusters, if he lacks civility, a big stick will not save him from trouble; and neither will speaking softly avail, if back of the softness there does not lie strength, power. In private life there are few beings more obnoxious than the man who is always loudly boasting; and if the boaster is not prepared to back up his words his position becomes absolutely contemptible. So it is with the nation. It is both foolish and undignified to indulge in undue self-glorification, and, above all, in loose-tongued denunciation of other peoples."

The big stick without the soft speech, in other words, is just a man shouting.

The speech is called "National Duties," and the rest of it is harder going: a defense of American rule in the Philippines in the language of civilization and barbarism, and of the taking of Dakota from the people who lived there. Both things are in the same address.

Twelve days later William McKinley was dead and Roosevelt was President of the United States.

The big stick without the soft speech, in other words, is just a man shouting.

The speech is called "National Duties," and the rest of it is harder going: a defense of American rule in the Philippines in the language of civilization and barbarism, and of the taking of Dakota from the people who lived there. Both things are in the same address.

#OTD in 1902, on the last morning of a New England tour, a streetcar ran into the President of the United States.

Roosevelt was in an open carriage outside Pittsfield, Massachusetts, with Governor Winthrop Murray Crane and his secretary George Cortelyou. An electric trolley came down the hill fast. William Craig, the Secret Service man riding with them, saw it coming and shouted.

The car struck the carriage. Roosevelt was thrown into the road. Cortelyou was concussed. Craig went under the wheels and was killed — the first Secret Service agent to die in the line of duty.

He was a Scot from Glasgow, six foot four, a champion broadswordsman who had spent twelve years in the Royal Horse Guards, some of it guarding Queen Victoria. He had been assigned to Roosevelt in Buffalo almost exactly a year earlier — days after standing on McKinley's detail the afternoon McKinley was shot.

Roosevelt got up, found his spectacles unbroken in the grass, and told the doctor to see to the others. Then he saw what was under the trolley. He went at the motorman with his fists up, and men had to get between them. Then he came back and knelt by the wheels.

"Poor Craig," he said. "How my children will feel."

He kept the rest of the day's stops but made no speeches. By evening he was on the presidential yacht, headed home.

The injury that mattered turned out not to be the face. A blow to his left leg abscessed over the following three weeks and needed emergency surgery in Indianapolis, which put him on crutches and cut short a second speaking trip. He had trouble with that leg for the rest of his life.

The motorman, Euclid Madden, pleaded guilty to manslaughter and was sentenced to six months in jail and a $300 fine.

Of Craig, Roosevelt said: "The man who was killed was one of whom I was fond and whom I greatly prized for his loyalty and faithfulness." Craig had been closest of all to four-year-old Quentin. They used to read the funny papers together.

#OTD in 1879, a twenty-year-old Theodore Roosevelt spent the day packing a canoe, and wrote down exactly what went in it.

"Spent the day preparing for my Munsungun trip; I shall go in a canoe, alone with Seawall. For provisions I took pork and hardtack & some flour; we have a shelter tent, two blankets & some cooking utensils; & one complete change of clothing each. I take 50 cartridges for the rifle and 100 for the shotgun. I shall only use moccasins."

Pork, hardtack, flour. A shelter tent. Two blankets. One change of clothes. A hundred and fifty rounds. No boots.

"Seawall" is Bill Sewall — William Wingate Sewall, a Maine guide thirteen years his senior who had been taking this asthmatic, nearsighted college boy into the woods and finding, to his own surprise, that he could keep up. Sewall's first impression, set down years later, was of "a thin, pale youngster with bad eyes and a weak heart."

They went up to Munsungan Lake, the two of them, and camped.

Five years later Roosevelt wrote to Sewall from Dakota Territory and asked him to come out and run a cattle ranch with him. Sewall had never seen the Badlands and did not want to go. He went anyway, with his nephew Wilmot Dow; the families followed, and Sewall's son was born at the Elkhorn. For two years they ran it. In 1886 Sewall and Dow were two of the three men who went down the ice-choked Little Missouri after the thieves who stole Roosevelt's boat.

He outlived him by eleven years. Around 1921, two years after Roosevelt died, Sewall walked back in to the shore of Munsungan Lake with Game Warden Walter Wood and a man named Russell Whitman, cut a blaze into a pine and built a cairn of stones at the foot of it, to mark the place where the two of them had camped. Somebody photographed it. The old man in the suspenders, leaning on the tree and watching the younger men stack the rocks, is Bill Sewall.

Gail and Doug, thanks for being number 100,000.

To number 100,001: the doors are open, and the light out here in September is worth the drive.

#OTD in 1905, at 3:47 in the afternoon, Russia and Japan signed a peace treaty in a shipyard building at Kittery, Maine. The Russo-Japanese War was over. The man who had spent the summer forcing it to happen was two hundred miles away and never once set foot in the room.

Theodore Roosevelt ran the Portsmouth conference from Sagamore Hill, his house at Oyster Bay — largely by going around the diplomats. He wrote to General Francis V. Greene the same day the treaty was signed:

"…only by disregarding the old conventional diplomatic methods… I communicated personally with the Czar, the Mikado, the Kaiser, Balfour, Rouvier, and so forth."

A month earlier he had put both delegations aboard the presidential yacht Mayflower off Oyster Bay and fed them a standing buffet — no seating plan, no head of the table — so that no one held the place of honor. Then he solved the impossible question of whose sovereign to toast first:

"Gentlemen: I propose a toast to which there will be no answer, and which I ask you to drink in silence, standing. I drink to the welfare and prosperity of the sovereigns and peoples of the two great nations whose representatives have met one another on this ship."

Japan gave up its claim to an indemnity. Russia gave up the southern half of Sakhalin. Four plenipotentiaries signed — Baron Komura Jutarō and Takahira Kogorō for Japan, Sergei Witte and Baron Roman Rosen for Russia — four copies, two in English and two in French. Witte was made a count on his return; the treaty was the reason.

In Tokyo, police blocked a protest rally at Hibiya Park against a peace many Japanese considered a humiliation. The city rioted. At least eleven people were killed and more than a thousand injured, and martial law was declared the next morning.

The following year Roosevelt became the first American to win a Nobel Prize in any category. He did not go to Norway for it — the American minister accepted on his behalf — and he did not deliver his Nobel lecture until 1910, more than a year after leaving office.

#OTD in 1901, at seven minutes past four in the afternoon, President William McKinley stood in the Temple of Music at the Pan-American Exposition in Buffalo, shaking hands with anyone who cared to shake his.

A good test of a museum: the teenager who didn't want to leave.

Michael M. Rosen brought his 19-year-old son to Medora in mid-August and wrote it up for the Washington Free Beacon, under a title worth the price of admission — "A Bull Moose Amid the Bison."

Rosen came prepared. Roosevelt caught him in high school, held him through the Edmund Morris volumes, and stayed with him long enough that he named his first son Theodore, in part for the president. The 19-year-old is that Theodore's younger brother, and by his father's account he "isn't the world's biggest fan of museums."

He "insisted we stay far longer than we had allocated to the visit."

Rosen singles out two highlights: the room devoted to the "Man in the Arena" speech, and the final exhibit of Roosevelt's own words, read aloud by a range of voices.

Then father and son drove out into Theodore Roosevelt National Park and ran straight into a herd of bison. Which is, more or less, the correct way to end the day.

His last line: "Bully for Medora, bully for TR, and bully for his astonishing legacy."

Thank you, Washington Free Beacon and Michael M. Rosen, for making the trip.

#OTD in 1897, the Assistant Secretary of the Navy went to sea to watch battleships shoot at things. He brought an artist along.

Theodore Roosevelt joined the North Atlantic Squadron about thirty miles east of the Virginia capes, aboard the dispatch boat Dolphin. Rear Admiral Montgomery Sicard's ships were at sub-calibre practice; on learning that Roosevelt wanted to see the heavy guns, Sicard suspended it and designated the new battleship Iowa, commissioned that June, to fire her batteries in his presence. Most of her crew had never heard the main battery fired. A whaleboat was put out of service, some skylights broke, and a door or two came off its hinges.

The artist was Frederic Remington, whose drawings had done more than anyone's to fix in the American mind what a cowboy looked like. Roosevelt had been using him for a decade — Remington illustrated Ranch Life and the Hunting-Trail in 1888 — and this time he wanted something else entirely. He wrote to him on 15 September:

"I wish I were with you out among the sage brush, the great brittle cottonwoods, and the sharply-channeled, barren buttes; but I am very glad at any rate to have had you along with the squadron; and I can't help looking upon you as an ally from henceforth on in trying to make the American people see the beauty and the majesty of our ships, and the heroic quality which lurks somewhere in all those who man and handle them."

To Henry Cabot Lodge he was simply happy: "Think of it, on the Atlantic Ocean, out of sight of land, going out to dinner to a battleship in evening dress without an overcoat!"

To Rudyard Kipling he reported that Remington "was very nearly blown up through incautiously getting too near the blast line of one of the 13-inch guns." Iowa's main battery was twelve-inch. The Assistant Secretary of the Navy got the caliber wrong.

Remington gave Harper's Weekly five drawings that year — a tug-of-war, winter at an army post, tarpon fishing, a wounded bull elk, and the horse show. Not one warship. Roosevelt was still nudging him in November: "we were all wishing that you would do something about the Navy some time." He never got his Navy pictures.

He got something else. Nine months later Remington was in Cuba with the army, and by the end of that year he had painted the charge of the Rough Riders. At Montauk that September, as the regiment prepared to muster out, Roosevelt's men presented him with a Remington bronze. He still had it fifteen years later: "Perhaps our most cherished possessions are a Remington bronze, 'The Bronco Buster,' given me by my men when the regiment was mustered out…"

#OTD in 1883, shortly after two in the morning, a twenty-four-year-old New York assemblyman stepped off a Northern Pacific train at Little Missouri, Dakota Territory, and stood in the dark.

Little Missouri was a handful of buildings on the west bank of the river. Medora, across the water, was five months old — the Marquis de Morès had founded it that April. The traveler hammered on the door of the Pyramid Park Hotel and dropped the name of Commander H. H. Gorringe, the retired naval officer who owned the old Army cantonment nearby, which was enough to end the argument. Upstairs was one long room with fourteen cots in it, known locally as the bull-pen. Thirteen were occupied. He paid two bits for the last one.

He had come to shoot a buffalo before there were none left to shoot, and he was nearly too late. The northern herd was in its last months; the final large herd on the northern plains would be destroyed that October, a few weeks after he arrived.

By morning he had a guide. He wrote to his wife Alice that same day about "a good looking hunter named Joe Ferris."

What followed was, by his own account, a fiasco — rain, wet blankets, biscuits gone soft, and bad shooting. "So far the trip had certainly not been a success," he wrote later, "although sufficiently varied as regards its incidents." Joe Ferris remembered a client who would not quit: "He could stand an awful lot of hard knocks, and he was always cheerful. You just couldn't knock him out of sorts." A neighbor, Lincoln Lang, put it less kindly: "He nearly killed poor Joe. He would not stop for anything."

He got his buffalo on 20 September. But the more consequential thing had happened two days earlier, on a log outside Gregor Lang's cabin, when he handed Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield a check for fourteen thousand dollars to go into the cattle business — more than his entire income for the year. Merrifield, decades later: "He handed us a check for fourteen thousand dollars, handed it right over to us on a verbal contract. He didn't have a scratch of a pen for it." Merrifield asked whether he wanted a receipt. "Oh, that's all right." A written contract followed nine days later, signed in St. Paul.

Twenty-seven years on, speaking at Fargo, he said it plainly: "I can never begin to say what I owe to North Dakota. It is not only that I never would have been president if it had not been for my experiences here in North Dakota…"

It started at two in the morning, in a fourteen-bunk room, with a man who had come to kill one animal.

#OTD in 1883, on his second day in Dakota Territory, Theodore Roosevelt rode about forty-five miles south down the Little Missouri to a cabin belonging to a man he had never met.

He had a horse now. The night before, at the Maltese Cross, he had tried to talk Sylvane Ferris and Bill Merrifield out of a buckskin mare named Nell, failed, and bought her instead. Joe Ferris, telling it to Hermann Hagedorn more than thirty-five years later:

"By gosh, he wanted that saddle horse so bad that we were afraid to let him have it. Why, we didn't know him from Job's off ox. We didn't know but what he'd ride away with it. But, say, he wanted that horse so blamed bad, that when he see we weren't going to let him have it, he offered to buy it for cash."

Hagedorn called the mare Roosevelt's "first physical hold on the Bad Lands."

They started at dawn — Joe driving the buckboard, Roosevelt alongside on Nell — fording the river again and again as it wandered across their path, and reached the mouth of the Little Cannonball at sunset. Gregor Lang's cabin stood in a cluster of cottonwoods fifty yards from where the creek met the river.

Lang was a Scot. The London financier Sir John Pender had bought into a Little Missouri cattle company that spring and sent Lang out to keep an eye on it; by September Lang was running a ranch of his own on Pender's money. He had a sixteen-year-old son named Lincoln, who remembered the arrival for the rest of his life:

"Aided by the beam of light showing through the cabin door, I could make out that he was a young man, who wore large conspicuous-looking glasses, through which I was being regarded with interest by a pair of twinkling eyes. Amply supporting them was the expansive grin overspreading his prominent, forceful lower face, plainly revealing a set of larger white teeth. Smiling teeth, yet withal conveying a strong suggestion of hang-and-rattle. The kind of teeth that are made to hold anything they once close upon…"

His father made the introduction. Lincoln remembered the reply too: "Dee-lighted to meet you, Lincoln!"

Then Joe Ferris, who had just driven a buckboard forty-five miles, went to bed, and the New Yorker and the Scotsman sat up talking cattle until midnight.

#OTD in 1907, Theodore Roosevelt set aside 2,262,624 acres of Alaska rainforest — over the objection of his own Land Office.

Six months earlier Congress had taken the power away from him. An amendment to an agriculture bill forbade any new forest reserve, or any addition to one, in Oregon, Washington, Idaho, Montana, Colorado or Wyoming "except by Act of Congress." In the two days before he signed that bill, Roosevelt signed thirty-two proclamations — twenty-one new reserves and eleven enlargements, about sixteen million acres — in those six states. Then he signed the bill.

The amendment did not name Alaska.

The Forest Service had wanted far more than it got. Inspector F. E. Olmsted recommended reserving essentially all of southeastern Alaska, and a map was drawn for a "Baranof National Forest." Richard Ballinger, Commissioner of the General Land Office, opposed creating any national forest in Alaska at all: the forests were not needed to protect a water supply, he argued, there was no fire hazard, and nothing needed replanting. His assistant commissioner, Fred Dennett, called the project a "conspiracy" to get around the ban on exporting Alaska timber. The map was withdrawn.

So W. A. Langille, the supervisor on the ground, drew a smaller one, and predicted: "The only objection to creation of the reserve will come from those who oppose the national forest policy on general principles."

He was wrong about that. Both Alaska territorial parties, Republican and Democratic, had adopted planks the year before demanding that the reserve already there be abolished.

Roosevelt signed anyway. Proclamation 772 set the land apart "for the use and benefit of the people." It states no acreage at all — every figure since has come from Land Office bookkeeping. Three weeks before he left office, on 16 February 1909, he added 8.7 million acres more.

The Tongass is now 16.7 million acres, the largest national forest in the country and the largest intact coastal temperate rainforest on earth. It is also Tlingit, Haida and Tsimshian homeland, and the proclamations do not mention them. In 1959 the U.S. Court of Claims held that their aboriginal title had never been extinguished and that the proclamations creating the Tongass were an uncompensated taking. Damages were awarded in 1968 — though the court struck the award for fishing rights, which its own earlier opinion had called the most valuable thing they lost. Congress extinguished the remaining claims in 1971.

#OTD in 1900, the Republican candidate for vice president crossed eastern South Dakota by rail — Flandreau at eight in the morning, Madison at half past nine, Sioux Falls at midday, Vermillion at half past six, Yankton by torchlight in the evening. Eleven stops in a single day, two of them across the line in Iowa.

It had rained hard the night before. Theodore M. Knappen, a Minneapolis Journal staff correspondent travelling with the party, wrote up the Madison stop:

"At Madison the governor and company were hustled into carriages and driven to the opera house, a boys' band running along the sidewalks thumping out a tune. 'And this reminds me of old times,' said the governor to the newspaper men. 'I feel at home now. The wide muddy street, the high sidewalks, the straggling stores. How I would like to take a team and go out on the prairies after chickens for a whole day.'"

The mud was real. The Saint Paul Globe reported that "the rain of the preceding night had rendered the streets so muddy that an outdoor reception was impossible," so the local committee moved him into the opera house instead of the stand by the depot.

Roosevelt had ranched in Dakota Territory from 1883 to 1886 — up on the Little Missouri, in what by 1900 was North Dakota, a state away from the street he was standing on.

Not everyone was charmed. The Madison Daily Leader, a Populist paper, covered the visit on the eleventh and reported that when the carriage came up the street and went back down again there was not a single cheer: "it might as well have been an ice-wagon." On the twelfth it reprinted Knappen's dispatch under the headline "THE PRETTY STORY," explaining that it would "afford us a text or two for the future." On the thirteenth: "Mr. Roosevelt's tour is not a triumph but a vote-begging fizzle." The state's larger papers saw a different day — the Sioux Falls Argus-Leader headlined its account "Veni! Vidi! Vici!"

He kept going. The tally the newspapers printed on Election Day: 21,209 miles, 567 towns, 24 states, 673 speeches. Historians have since put the number of stops lower. One surviving day from an aide's timetable has seven speeches in it plus two solid hours of speaking after supper, with Sir Walter Scott and a book on birds wedged into the gaps.

He had told Mark Hanna at the outset how hard he could be worked: "I am as strong as a bull moose, and you can use me to the limit, taking heed of but one thing and that is my throat."

#OTD in 1906, from Sagamore Hill, Theodore Roosevelt finished a book he had not enjoyed and wrote to Henry Cabot Lodge about it.

The book was Winston Churchill's two-volume life of his father, Lord Randolph, published that January. Churchill was thirty-one and had sat in the House of Commons since 1901. Roosevelt was president.

"I have been over Winston Churchill's life of his father. I dislike the father and dislike the son, so I may be prejudiced. Still, I feel that, while the biographer and his subject possess some real farsightedness… yet they both possess or possessed such levity, lack of sobriety, lack of permanent principle, and inordinate thirst for that cheap form of admiration which is given to notoriety, as to make them poor public servants."

Lodge wrote back four days later, admitting he had not read the book: "The son I know; I have met him several times. He is undoubtedly clever but conceited to a degree which it is hard to express either in words or figures."

The strange part is how it started. In December 1900 Churchill was twenty-six and lecturing across America. Roosevelt — then governor of New York and vice president-elect — could not get to the New York lecture, and said so with real regret: "I am really sorry as I am a great admirer of Mr. Churchill's books, and should very much like to have a chance to meet him socially."

They dined at the Executive Mansion in Albany late that month. Something soured. Roosevelt's own account, seven months later: "I saw the Englishman Winston Churchill here and although he is not an attractive fellow, I was interested in some of the things he said."

They never met again. In 1910, sent to represent the United States at Edward VII's funeral, he wrote: "I have refused to meet Winston Churchill, being able to avoid any scandal by doing so."

Then, on 22 August 1914, to his English friend Arthur Lee: "I have never liked Winston Churchill, but, in view of what you tell me about his admirable conduct and nerve in mobilizing the Fleet, I do wish that if it comes your way you would extend to him my congratulations on his action."

Churchill seems never to have registered any of it. In 1918 he proposed sending Theodore Roosevelt to Moscow as the Allies' envoy to Lenin.

#OTD in 1887, at a quarter past two in the morning, Edith Roosevelt gave birth to a son at Sagamore Hill. They named him Theodore.

He grew up small and highly strung. Edith's verdict, when he was seven: "Ted grows like a Century Plant, that is, not at all visibly."

In the year he turned nine, his father came home from town with a rifle. It was a Flobert — a parlor gun, the sort built for target shooting indoors. The Flobert cartridge carried no powder charge at all; the primer was the whole propellant, which is why such a thing could be fired in a bedroom. Ted told the rest himself, decades later:

"At once I made for his room, where I found him just preparing for his bath. The rifle was standing in a corner. Of course I fell on it with delight. He was as much excited as I was. I wanted to see it fired to make sure it was a real rifle. That presented a difficulty. It would be too dark to shoot after supper and Father was not dressed to go out at the moment. He took it, slipped a cartridge into the chamber, and making me promise not to tell Mother, fired it into the ceiling. The report was slight, the smoke hardly noticeable, and the hole made in the ceiling so small that our sin was not detected."

Ted spelled it "Flaubert," like the novelist. Most historians have quietly corrected him.

Two years on, the boy was ten and racked with headaches and nervous exhaustion, and the doctors were, in his father's words, "utterly unable to find out the ultimate cause of the trouble." Edith knew the cause. She put it to an old friend who was a physician, Dr. Alexander Lambert, and Lambert examined Ted, agreed with her, and put it to Roosevelt in writing: the boy was being pushed too hard, by him.

Roosevelt surrendered. "Hereafter I shall never press Ted either in body or mind. The fact is that the little fellow, who is peculiarly dear to me, has bidden fair to be all the things I would like to have been and wasn't, and it has been a great temptation to push him."

He never entirely managed it. But he wrote it down.

#OTD in 1901, at a quarter past two in the morning, William McKinley died in Buffalo of the wounds he had taken eight days earlier. Theodore Roosevelt became President of the United States in a wagon, on an Adirondack road, in the dark — and did not know it for three hours.

He had spent the previous day climbing Mount Marcy, the highest peak in New York, on the strength of the doctors' assurances that the President was recovering. He wrote about the moment that ended:

"After reaching the top I had descended a few hundred feet to a shelf of land where there was a little lake, when I saw a guide coming out of the woods on our trail from below. I felt at once that he had bad news, and, sure enough, he handed me a telegram saying that the President's condition was much worse and that I must come to Buffalo immediately."

The telegram itself said only that McKinley's condition gave rise to "the gravest apprehension." The rest was what Roosevelt read in the sight of a man climbing a mountain toward him.

He left the club at Tahawus at 11:31 that night: thirty-five miles of dark, rain-washed road in relays of horses — the club superintendent David Hunter to the Lower Works, Orrin Kellogg on to Aiden Lair, and Mike Cronin the last sixteen miles behind two black Morgans, in an hour and forty-one minutes. Two miles short of the station they stopped to let the horses blow, and Roosevelt straightened his tie, saying there might be notables waiting at the depot. They reached North Creek at 5:22 a.m., and his secretary, William Loeb, handed him John Hay's telegram from Washington.

In Buffalo the first suggestion had been to swear him in at the Milburn house, where McKinley's body lay upstairs. It was objected to as unsuitable. Roosevelt went there only to pay his respects, and took the oath somewhere else.

At 3:32 that afternoon, in the library of his friend Ansley Wilcox's house on Delaware Avenue, in a borrowed frock coat and with no Bible, he took the oath from Judge John R. Hazel of the U.S. District Court, before a small company of cabinet officers, judges and reporters. At 42, he was the youngest person ever to hold the office.

Before the oath he answered Secretary of War Elihu Root: "it shall be my aim to continue absolutely unbroken the policy of President McKinley for the peace, the prosperity and the honor of our beloved country."

The house is still there, at 641 Delaware Avenue. It is the Theodore Roosevelt Inaugural National Historic Site.

#OTD in 1898, at Camp Wikoff on Montauk Point, the Rough Riders took down their colors, turned in their horses and rifles, shook hands, and scattered.

There was no ceremony. Muster-out was paperwork, and it took three days: troop by troop to the paymaster's table, last pay, discharge papers, and a train to New York. The farewell had come first, on the thirteenth, when the regiment formed a hollow square and gave their colonel a Remington bronze. The fifteenth was the end of the process — "the day," Roosevelt wrote, "which marked the close of the four months' life of a regiment of as gallant fighters as ever wore the United States uniform."

In those four months the 1st U.S. Volunteer Cavalry lost more enlisted men than any other regiment in the cavalry division: twenty-three killed in action, three more dead of wounds, twenty dead of disease, and more than a hundred wounded. Of the twenty-eight field and line officers who landed in Cuba on 22 June, ten were killed or wounded in the nine days that followed.

Roosevelt's own catalogue of the regiment includes professional gamblers and "no less than four" Baptist or Methodist clergymen — "and proved first-class fighters, too, by the way." Cherokee, Chickasaw, Choctaw and Creek men came from the Indian Territory. Not all the Indian troopers did: William Pollock, a Pawnee from Oklahoma Territory, was an artist and a penman who became the regimental clerk in Cuba. After the last man had filed past to shake his hand at the square, Roosevelt said: "I made Pollock, the Pawnee, smile today, and I do not believe anyone ever saw him smile before."

Standing in that square were some two hundred troopers of the 9th and 10th Cavalry — the Black regulars who had held the flanks at Las Guasimas and gone up Kettle Hill alongside the regiment. Roosevelt turned to his own men and said of them: "between you and the other cavalry regiments there is a tie which we trust will never be broken."

One Rough Rider was not at Montauk to see any of it. Jesse Langdon of Fargo, sixteen years old and usually called the youngest man in the regiment, had first met Roosevelt in Medora at the age of five. Turned away for being underage in 1898, he rode a freight train to Washington with ten dollars and caught Roosevelt coming down the stairs of a recruiting office. Asked whether he could ride a horse, he said: "I can ride anything that's got hair on it!" By September he was home in Fargo with fever. He outlived every other man in the regiment, dying in 1975.

Roosevelt ended his own account of them with a question: "Is it any wonder that I loved my regiment?"

#OTD in 1900, a Sunday, Theodore Roosevelt's campaign train stopped at Medora and he went for a ride.

He had been arguing with himself about it for a week. A Chicago Record correspondent travelling with the party wrote it up that day: "The rough rider has been puzzled for a week over the question whether to stop for a handshake today with his old neighbors of the cattle region and run the risk of raising a protest about sabbath breaking or to lock himself up in his car, run past the scenes of what he calls his happiest days and incur the suspicion of his former comrades that he had 'passed them up.' He decided in favor of his comrades of the days when he was a deputy under Sheriff 'Hell-Roaring Bill Jones.'"

He made no speeches. His rule for the trip was no politics on a Sunday and no running through a town while services were on, and when the brass bands started greeting him with "Hot Time in the Old Town," he wired ahead: "Suppress the band or make it play sacred music." At Dickinson the bandmaster, searching a meager repertoire for anything with a suggestion of Sabbath solemnity, settled on "Georgia Camp Meetin'."

At Medora the special was side-tracked to let the regular train pass. Joe Ferris — who had guided him to his first buffalo in 1883 — had come up to Bismarck to meet him and ridden west with him. Old Mrs. Roberts took his hand and would not let go: "God bless you! You are just the same as when you left us."

Then he got on a bronco, born and busted in the valley of the Little Missouri, and galloped with his old mates up onto the plateau above the town, where the correspondent had him looking out at the red walls above his old Maltese Cross range. Sitting up there on the horse, he said it:

"Here the romance of my life began."

Joe Ferris told him: "Governor, I don't believe you'd ever done so well if you hadn't bucked up agin the real thing with us first." Roosevelt: "That's exactly right, Joe. I had studied a lot about men and things before I saw you fellows, but it was only when I came out here that I began to know anything or to measure men right."

Afterward, as the train ran west through the badlands, he stood alone on the rear platform with the door shut behind him and the porter told to keep visitors away.

#OTD in 1903, on the forty-first anniversary of the battle, Theodore Roosevelt stood on the field at Antietam in the rain and accepted a monument.

New Jersey's veterans had come down the day before on a state-funded excursion train and overnighted in Hagerstown. Survivors of the 13th New Jersey formed a hollow square at Antietam station to meet the Presidential train and escort him in. Over four hundred veterans of the battle were on the field that day, in a crowd of thousands. Governor Franklin Murphy presented the monument — he had been on that ground before, as a sixteen-year-old corporal in Company A of the 13th New Jersey who had given his age as eighteen to enlist. Antietam was the first combat of his life.

Forty feet of granite, and at the top, in bronze, a figure with an upraised sword: Captain Hugh C. Irish of the 13th New Jersey. The commission's report, read aloud that morning, placed him as the first man killed in his regiment, within a hundred yards of where the monument stands.

Roosevelt spoke about what the day had decided:

"Moreover, in its ultimate effects this battle was of momentous and even decisive importance; for when it had ended and Lee had retreated south of the Potomac, Lincoln forthwith published that immortal paper, the preliminary declaration of emancipation; the paper which decided that the Civil War, besides being a war for the preservation of the Union, should be a war for the emancipation of the slave, so that from that time onward the causes of Union and of Freedom, of national greatness and individual liberty, were one and the same."

Lincoln issued the Preliminary Emancipation Proclamation five days after the battle, on 22 September 1862.

The sky opened just as he began. William H. Rau photographed the President reading from his manuscript over a field of open umbrellas; the stereograph card is captioned, plainly, "President Roosevelt finishing his address in the rain."

#OTD in 1880, a twenty-one-year-old shooting grouse in western Minnesota had a bad night, and wrote it down.

"We had very much the best days sport we have had; there were innumerable grouse, though they were wild. But I had to sit up most of last night with the asthma, I was so troubled with continual attacks of colic that I could hardly walk, and it rained most of the day, so I shot badly; Elliott however did splendidly. We have had pretty good fare and accomadations up here, so far, and great fun; but I shall be perfectly overjoyed to get back to Alice."

Two days earlier he had written "I am now feeling in superb health and strength." Two days later: "now I am feeling in superb health." The attack came in between, on the night of the seventeenth, and he sat up through it.

The asthma never left him. The story that he beat it by will and exercise is one he half-encouraged; the medical record doesn't support it, and he had serious attacks well into adulthood.

"Elliott" is his younger brother, twenty years old. Theodore kept the game tally himself, in a table headed T, E and Total — and he kept it honestly on his bad days. On the grouse Elliott beat him badly over the trip, 163 to 95; on this particular day, 42 birds to 19. Across everything they shot, Theodore finished ahead, 203 to 201. Elliott would become the father of Eleanor Roosevelt.

Alice is Alice Hathaway Lee. They married on 27 October 1880, his twenty-second birthday.

#OTD in 1885, a Bismarck jury took ten minutes to acquit the Marquis de Morès of murder.

It was his third time answering for the killing of Riley Luffsey, a nineteen-year-old hunter shot on a cow trail near Little Missouri on 26 June 1883. Two earlier hearings had discharged him. Luffsey's surviving companion, Dutch Wannegan, testified that the first shot came from the brush and that they never returned fire. The Marquis and his men testified it was self-defense. He did not have to take the stand and chose to; the Tribune's summary of his testimony carried the line the case has never shaken off — that as the firing was general, no one could know who killed Luffsey.

The trial ran a week at Bismarck, moved there from Mandan on a change of venue that set off indignation meetings and a petition to remove the judge. On the last day of testimony the prosecutor was fined $250 for contempt, wrote a check on the spot, and carried on. Closing arguments finished before noon on Saturday. The judge charged the jury between one and two.

The Bismarck Weekly Tribune ran the result under a headline that needs no help:

MARQUIS ACQUITTED
The Jury Return After an Absence of Ten Minutes and Render a Verdict of Acquittal

One ballot was taken.

Sometime that September, on his way east, Roosevelt stopped at the jail. Hermann Hagedorn, whose 1921 book is the only source for the story, puts it at Mandan just after a mob shot up the jail; Dresden puts it at Bismarck on the eve of trial. What Hagedorn recorded: the Marquis's secretary under the bed, and the Marquis sitting on the edge of it, smoking.

The verdict settled one question and left the other open. Medora turned out to cheer him home. The men who had opposed him from the day he arrived never changed their minds.

De Morès left the Badlands the next year. In France he became one of Paris's most violent antisemitic agitators — an ally of Édouard Drumont at La Libre Parole, and the man who killed a Jewish French army officer, Captain Armand Mayer, in a duel in June 1892. He was killed in the Sahara in 1896, betrayed by his own hired guides.

#OTD in 1905, Theodore Roosevelt signed an order that the Medal of Honor could no longer arrive in the mail.

Before it, some had. The Senate's own history of the medal records that some were "returned to the War and Navy Departments because the recipients who had earned them had been discharged and their whereabouts were unknown" — the highest decoration in American arms, come back marked address unknown.

Executive Order 352-A:

"The presentation of a Medal of Honor to an officer or enlisted man in the military service… will always be made with formal and impressive ceremonial. The recipient will, when practicable, be ordered to Washington, D.C., and the presentation will be made by the President, as Commander in Chief, or by such representative as the President may designate."

Presidents had done it in person before — Grant twice. Roosevelt made it the rule.

Not quite four months later came the first White House presentation under the order: Captain James Robb Church, the Rough Riders' assistant surgeon, who at Las Guásimas — where the 10th Cavalry fought alongside them — carried wounded troopers off the firing line on his back, five times, under fire.

Roosevelt had wanted one himself. After Cuba he lobbied hard and lost. "I don't ask this as a favor—I ask it as a right," he wrote Lodge. Elsewhere: "I am entitled to the Medal of Honor and I want it." A board declined. At Church's ceremony he volunteered, unprompted, that the letters he'd written had been written before he was president, and that since taking office he had held no communication with the military authorities on the subject. Two years after signing the order, in 1907, he refused to join the Medal of Honor Club: "looking back on it now, I feel that the board which declined to award it took exactly the right position."

The order itself began elsewhere — with Major William E. Birkhimer, a Medal of Honor man himself, who in December 1904 wrote the War Department that the medal deserved "formality and solemnity of circumstance." There is no record that Roosevelt's own disappointment was on his mind when he signed it. It is hard not to notice.

His medal was awarded in 2001 — in the Roosevelt Room, which stands on the site of his West Wing office.

#OTD in 1907, Theodore Roosevelt sat down at Sagamore Hill and wrote to his thirteen-year-old son, who had left for boarding school the morning before.

"BLESSED ARCHIEKINS:

We felt dreadfully homesick as you and Kermit drove away; when we pass along the bay front we always think of the dory; and we mourn dear little Skip, although perhaps it was as well the little doggie should pass painlessly away, after his happy little life; for the little fellow would have pined for you."

Skip had come out of John Goff's hound pack on a Colorado bear hunt in 1905 and decided on his own that he belonged to Roosevelt. "There is a very cunning little dog named Skip, belonging to John Goff's pack, who has completely adopted me," TR wrote Kermit from Glenwood Springs. "I think I shall take him home to Archie." On the hunt Skip rode in front of Roosevelt's saddle and slept on the foot of his bed, "growling defiance at anything that came near." He came back to Washington and lived in the White House. Then he transferred the whole of his allegiance to Archie and went everywhere the boy went, including out in the dory.

He was run over by an automobile at Oyster Bay the day before Archie left. Roosevelt had written it plainly to Nannie Lodge the day before this letter: "you can imagine Archie's grief — and indeed, for the matter of that, the grief of the rest of us. So poor little black Skip was buried under the stone that bears the names of the dogs for which we have cared the most."

To his son, the next day, he called it passing painlessly away. Archie had been at Sagamore Hill when it happened.

The rest of the letter is a father filling a silence. The football suit will be sent on. Of course it will all be new and rather hard at first. The house is "put up," everything wrapped in white that can be, and all the rugs off the floors. And then the last line:

"Quentin is reduced to the secret service men for steady companionship."

The stone is still at Sagamore Hill. It is headed "Faithful Friends."

#OTD in 1911, Theodore Roosevelt wrote four lines to a New York political journalist about a ballot in California.

"Dear Mr. Harvier:

The trouble with my friends the Progressives, with whom I am in such hearty sympathy is that they tend to try to do too much. It is a great mistake to have too many things voted on at an election.

Sincerely yours,"

Ernest Harvier had sent him a clipping three days before: "Judging from the enclosed, the progressives of California have, so to speak, considerable on hand for next month."

They did. On 10 October 1911, Californians voted on twenty-three constitutional amendments at once — the initiative, the referendum, the recall of elected officials, workers' compensation, railroad regulation, and woman suffrage. Twenty-two of the twenty-three passed. Suffrage carried by 3,587 votes out of nearly a quarter of a million, and made California the sixth state to adopt it.

A note on the word. "My friends the Progressives," in September 1911, does not mean the party of 1912 — that did not exist yet. It means the insurgent progressive Republicans, whose league — the National Progressive Republican League, formed that January — Roosevelt had been asked to join and had declined. He commended its principles but would not sign on, wary of both La Follette's candidacy and of how far its most insistent backers meant to go.

Seven days later he wrote Harvier again, and the second letter is the other half of the first:

"All that the open primary can do is to give the people a chance to get the men they want. If they do not take advantage of the chance, why! it is their fault, and that is all there is to it. No governmental device of this kind will ever give good citizenship."

Both letters are in the Library of Congress. Five months after the first one, Roosevelt declared against Taft.

#OTD in 1890, Theodore Roosevelt got back to Medora from Yellowstone and wrote to Henry Cabot Lodge the same day.

"I have just reached here, our party having separated after a really lovely two weeks in the Yellowstone Park."

The party was his wife Edith, his sisters Anna — Bamie — and Corinne, Douglas Robinson, Robert Munro Ferguson, and Lodge's sixteen-year-old son George — Bay — who had skipped Yellowstone altogether to stay in the badlands and hunt. Roosevelt found him waiting at Medora: "rugged, hearty and healthy; he had killed three antelope, and had not had his clothes off since I left; so he is thoroughly happy."

They had come out three weeks earlier. Corinne wrote it down:

"Our train drew up, or I should say, approximately drew up, to the little station at Medora at four o'clock in the morning, in one of the most frightful storms that I ever remember. Rain fell in torrents, and we had to get out on an embankment composed of such slippery mud that before we actually plodded to the station, our feet and legs were encased in glutinous slime."

Then some thirty-five miles north to the Elkhorn by wagon. "We forded the 'Little Missouri' River twenty-three times on the way to the ranch-house," Corinne wrote, "and as the banks of the river were extremely steep, it was always a question as to whether we could go fast enough down one bank to get sufficient impetus to enable us to go through the river and up the very steep bank on the other side."

Six days at the ranch. Afterward Roosevelt wrote to Edith's mother: "I have rarely seen Edith enjoy anything more than she did the six days at my ranch, and the trip through Yellowstone Park; and she looks just as well and young and pretty and happy as she did four years ago when I married her."

So far as her biographer records, Edith never saw the badlands again.

Roosevelt stayed on into October, hunting with Bay and sitting up one night to fight a prairie fire. Then, on 20 October, he wrote to Bill Sewall — the Maine woodsman who had built the ranch house and gone home four years before:

"This is the last year I shall keep the ranch house open; I have just parted with Merrifield. Sylvane will take care of the cattle now."

#OTD in 1906 — a hundred and twenty years ago today — Theodore Roosevelt created the first national monument in the country. He signed it at Sagamore Hill — the document carries the formula "Done at the City of Washington" — and there is no evidence he ever stood at the place.

Proclamation 658 set aside 1,152.91 acres in Crook County, Wyoming, around a column of rock the government called Devils Tower. The reason is in the document:

"the lofty and isolated rock in the State of Wyoming, known as the 'Devils Tower,' situated upon the public lands owned and controlled by the United States is such an extraordinary example of the effect of erosion in the higher mountains as to be a natural wonder and an object of historic and great scientific interest"

The Antiquities Act had been law fifteen weeks. Archaeologists pushed it through Congress to stop looters digging up ruins in the Southwest, and it held any monument to "the smallest area compatible with the proper care and management of the objects to be protected." Roosevelt's first use of it was not a ruin. It was a rock. Just over fifteen months later he used the same authority on the Grand Canyon.

The name is the older story. Most maps from 1857 to 1901 call it Bear Lodge. It is Mato Tipila to the Lakota; Bear's Lodge, Bear's House, Bear's Tipi and Bear Peak to the Cheyenne; Bear's Tipi to the Arapahoe; Aloft on a Rock and Tree Rock to the Kiowa. More than twenty tribes hold the place sacred. Their accounts differ nation to nation — the Park Service calls them oral histories and sacred narratives — and a bear, and the marks of its claws, runs through many.

The current name traces to one sentence. Col. Richard Irving Dodge led an expedition there in 1875 and wrote afterward: "The Indians call this shaft 'The Bad God's Tower,' a name adopted, with proper modification, by our surveyors." The Park Service: "It is suspected that a bad translation led the men to confuse the words for bear and bad god."

The name is contested today. A 2014 proposal asked the U.S. Board on Geographic Names to rename the rock and the town Bear Lodge; bills in Congress have sought to keep the current name; the question is undecided, and it is not the Park Service's to settle.

One more thing, for anyone reading this in Medora: the Little Missouri, the river that cut our badlands, rises about fifteen miles west of the tower, under the Missouri Buttes. It drains the other way — the tower stands above the Belle Fourche.

Roosevelt signed two routine forest-reserve proclamations the same day — Shasta in California, Long Pine in Montana. The third was the first national monument in American history.

#OTD in 1900, on a day that ran to eleven speeches, Theodore Roosevelt was carried off a platform in Boulder by a college football team.

He was governor of New York and William McKinley's running mate, working Colorado by rail — Eaton, Greeley, Fort Collins, Loveland, Berthoud, Longmont, Niwot, Boulder, and then Denver. The Indianapolis Journal's correspondent wrote it up the next morning:

"At Boulder a large out-of-door meeting was held near the station, situated in a picturesque valley, the sharp peaks of the nearby Rocky mountains, cloud capped and solemn, surrounding the city. At the conclusion of his short address Governor Roosevelt was pulled from the platform by the students forming the football team of the State University, which is situated here, and carried into his car on their shoulders over the heads of the people."

Then the team went back to the practice field. When his train rolled past, they lined up and put a place kick into the air after it.

He reached Denver at five, escorted by about a hundred mounted Spanish-American War veterans. Rain washed out the parade and the meeting on the capitol grounds, so he spoke indoors three times instead — Coliseum Hall, the Broadway Theater, Windsor Hall. That made eleven for the day, and the same correspondent added a detail worth keeping: "In addition to the eleven speeches which Governor Roosevelt made to-day he has had considerable executive business to attend to, being all the time in close touch with the executive office at Albany, both by wire and by mail."

He slept twelve miles out of town at a senator's house, with the Lodges.

From the train that day, to his sister Corinne: "I have had a very hard trip, but the last ten days I have rather enjoyed… Otherwise I do nothing but fester in the car and elbow to and from stagings where I address my audiences."

#OTD in 1900, a man at Victor, Colorado struck Theodore Roosevelt in the chest with a six-foot length of lumber. He went back out on the rear platform of his train and waved.

He was McKinley's running mate, working the Cripple Creek gold district by rail. The heckling started with his first words. From the New-York Tribune's account the next morning:

"A voice cried: 'What about the rotten beef?' The Governor replied: 'I ate it, and you will never get near enough to be hit with a bullet, or within five miles of it!'"

That was the embalmed-beef scandal of the Cuban campaign, and it was the friendliest exchange of the day. Leaving the hall on foot, in a street the Tribune put at "probably one thousand or fifteen hundred" people, he was hit in the breast with a six-foot piece of lumber — a scantling, the papers called it — that had been carrying a banner. Then rocks, rotten potatoes, eggs. Papers disagreed about who knocked the man down. Roosevelt took a kick on the knee that had swelled over the kneecap by the next day.

Back at the train he would not stay in the car. He went out on the rear platform, where the stones were still coming. Sherman Bell, who had served under him in Cuba, took hold of his shoulders. The Indianapolis Journal:

"'Come away, Colonel, come away,' entreated Sherman Bell, tugging at his shoulders… 'Stand aside, sir. I am your colonel, sir,' the Governor said, and Bell stepped back. 'Hurrah, hurrah,' shouted the Governor, leaning over the railing, waving his hand, and laughing like a boy on a toboggan slide."

No one was ever identified or arrested for it. People in Victor said afterward that the men who did it were not from Victor.

And from Nebraska that same night, the head of the ticket he was campaigning against:

"There can be no justification for a resort to violence in this country, and those who resort to it injure the cause which they represent." — William Jennings Bryan

"A voice cried: 'What about the rotten beef?' The Governor replied: 'I ate it, and you will never get near enough to be hit with a bullet, or within five miles of it!'"

That was the embalmed-beef scandal of the Cuban campaign, and it was the friendliest exchange of the day. Leaving the hall on foot, in a street the Tribune put at "probably one thousand or fifteen hundred" people, he was hit in the breast with a six-foot piece of lumber — a scantling, the papers called it — that had been carrying a banner. Then rocks, rotten potatoes, eggs. Papers disagreed about who knocked the man down. Roosevelt took a kick on the knee that had swelled over the kneecap by the next day.

Back at the train he would not stay in the car. He went out on the rear platform, where the stones were still coming. Sherman Bell, who had served under him in Cuba, took hold of his shoulders. The Indianapolis Journal:

"'Come away, Colonel, come away,' entreated Sherman Bell, tugging at his shoulders… 'Stand aside, sir. I am your colonel, sir,' the Governor said, and Bell stepped back. 'Hurrah, hurrah,' shouted the Governor, leaning over the railing, waving his hand, and laughing like a boy on a toboggan slide."

No one was ever identified or arrested for it. People in Victor said afterward that the men who did it were not from Victor.

And from Nebraska that same night, the head of the ticket he was campaigning against:

"There can be no justification for a resort to violence in this country, and those who resort to it injure the cause which they represent." — William Jennings Bryan

#OTD in 1876 — a hundred and fifty years ago today — a seventeen-year-old whose whole schooling amounted to a few months in a New York classroom arrived in Cambridge to begin at Harvard.

His father saw him off from the little station at Syosset, on Long Island. It was his sister Corinne's fifteenth birthday.

His preparation had been Arthur Cutler's, at home, and he arrived knowing exactly one member of his class, and him only slightly. What was waiting for him was his other sister's work. Bamie had gone up to Cambridge that summer, looked at the ground-floor rooms still open in the Yard, decided the damp would be bad for his asthma, and took him a second-floor room in a boardinghouse at 16 Winthrop Street instead. She had it papered and carpeted before he came.

He wrote to his mother:

"When I arrived here on Wednesday night I found a fire burning in the grate, and the room looking just as cosy and comfortable as it could look."

The 27th of September 1876 was a Wednesday.

Three days later, to Bamie: "When I get my pictures and books, I do not think there will be a room in College more handsome." He lived in that room all four years.

The asthma that had run his childhood let him alone that whole first autumn but for one slight attack in November. The only thing he was treated for was measles, and not until February.

His own verdict, written thirty-seven years later:

"In the fall of 1876 I entered Harvard, graduating in 1880. I thoroughly enjoyed Harvard, and I am sure it did me good, but only in the general effect, for there was very little in my actual studies which helped me in after life."

He turned eighteen a month after he got there.

#OTD in 1902, a surgeon opened the President's shin, scraped the bone, and left the wound unstitched so it could drain. Roosevelt was awake for it.

Three weeks earlier a trolley car had run into the presidential carriage at Pittsfield, Massachusetts, killing William Craig — the first Secret Service agent to die in the line of duty. Roosevelt was thrown clear with a bruised face and a bruised left shin. The shin was what would not heal. On 23 September, in the middle of a western speaking tour, surgeons at St. Vincent's in Indianapolis drew two ounces of fluid off the bone and sent him home. The rest of the tour was cancelled, and in Washington he was put in a wheeled chair.

Five days later it was worse. The White House was being rebuilt, so the family was living at 22 Jackson Place on Lafayette Square, and on the afternoon of Sunday the 28th the Surgeon General of the Navy, Presley Rixey, operated there — a two-inch incision over the tibia, the bone scraped smooth, the wound left open to drain. Cocaine around the site. No general anaesthetic. (Edmund Morris adds that Roosevelt let himself be half-anaesthetized with whiskey.)

Edith wrote to Kermit, just started at Groton, the same day. Her sentence is the whole story:

"made a gash nearly two inches long and scraped his shin bone… and as soon as it was over he was lifted back into his wheeled chair and came into the sitting room"

— where, she reported, he was already reading.

He stayed in that chair for weeks. Five days later he was still in it, in a blue striped robe with his left leg propped up, when the anthracite coal operators and the miners' president came to Jackson Place. The country was facing a winter without coal, and that meeting is where the ending of it began.

Six years on he wrote to Kermit about the leg: "The shock permanently damaged the bone, and if anything happens there is always a chance of trouble which would be serious."

It gave him trouble for the rest of his life.

#OTD in 1905, the President of the United States wrote to the president of Harvard to ask whether anything could be done about the photographers chasing his son around the Yard.

Theodore Roosevelt Jr. was eighteen years and sixteen days old and had been in his rooms a matter of days. The Washington Times had run him the day before under the headline "CAMERA FIENDS CHASE TEDDY, J.": "He was pursued by camera men, who snapped him wherever they got an opportunity… Roosevelt was very nervous, and did his best to keep out of range."

His father wrote to Charles W. Eliot from Oyster Bay:

"…they have been trying to take kodak pictures of him as he walked about the yard, and I suppose they will make similar attempts if he goes on the football field. I am inclined to tell him, if he sees any man taking a photograph of him, to run up and smash the camera, but I do not like to do this if you would disapprove."

About himself he was flat: "I care less than nothing about what they do or say about me, for I am entirely competent to defend myself and I am past the stage where they can do me any material damage…" About the boy he asked, plainly, "Is there no way he can be protected?"

What had set him off was a story about money. "They published the statement that he had a room in Claverly, thereby giving the impression that he had begun with a splurge." His defence was that the room was a small one — and it was. But Claverly Hall stood on Mount Auburn Street, and the Evening Star had already told its readers what that meant: "the best appointed dormitory of 'The Gold Coast' or 'Millionaires' Row.'" The same story noted, pointedly, that his father had lately been telling students to live in the plainest style.

What Eliot made of it is not recorded.

Ted made the freshman eleven that autumn and broke his nose against Yale. The following spring, with Ted on academic probation, his father wrote to him: "If you cannot study at Claverly (and I bitterly regret that I ever engaged you a room there) hire a quiet room outside of college and I will pay for it."

#OTD in 1899, thirty thousand men marched through a triumphal arch in New York City. The arch was made of plaster, and it was gone within a year.

The city had been at it for two days. On the 29th, Admiral George Dewey's flagship led a naval parade up the North River. On the 30th he came ashore, and the land parade formed at 122nd Street and Riverside Drive and started south at a quarter past eleven — the New-York Tribune noted it was only fifteen minutes behind time — and ran some six miles south to Washington Square.

Theodore Roosevelt was forty years old and nine months into his one term as governor of New York. He rode on horseback, in civilian clothes, at the head of the New York State troops, his adjutant general at his side. Major General Charles F. Roe rode far ahead of him, acting as grand marshal. The Tribune: "The Governor sat on his horse like a soldier, and even in citizen's garb showed that he had worn a sword." At the Washington Arch, where the parade ended, he swung out of the column with General Roe and reviewed the rest of it going by. He left a little before the last of it.

The arch is the part almost nobody remembers. Charles R. Lamb designed it on the model of the Arch of Titus, and the National Sculpture Society put twenty-eight sculptors to work covering it. It stood at Fifth Avenue and Twenty-fourth Street, and it was built of staff — plaster over a wooden frame — because everyone assumed the money would be raised to rebuild it in marble.

The money was not raised. Estimates for a permanent arch ran into the hundreds of thousands of dollars, and the subscription fell well short. The arch came down in 1900.

The Sun's banner headline the next morning was "SEVEN MILE THRONG." The Tribune put it this way: "There never were such crowds of people in New-York."

Manila Bay had been in May of the year before. The fighting in the Philippines was not over.

#OTD in 1902, Edith Roosevelt walked through the White House for the first time in nearly four months. It was still full of scaffolding.

The family had moved out in June. McKim, Mead & White had the greenhouses on the west terrace pulled down, the state dining room enlarged to seat more than a hundred, and the president's offices moved out of the White House proper for the first time, into a new wing to the west.

She spent about three hours there on the 1st with her daughter Alice and her social secretary, Belle Hagner. Superintendent French walked them through; the Evening Star puts the architect Charles McKim in the party as well. They came in at the main entrance on the north front, along an aisle rigged from crash stretched on the scaffolding, across new marble tiling swept clear and bright. The Washington Times reported the private dining room's stucco practically finished under its new dome-shaped ceiling, garnet hangings already up in the Red Parlor, and the stucco eagles with their flaring wings drawing praise from the party. And then he hears himself, and turns the letter around:

"There! you will think this a dreadfully preaching letter! I suppose I have a natural tendency to preach just at present because I am overwhelmed with my work. I enjoy being President, and I like to do the work and have my hand on the lever. #OTD in 1902, Theodore Roosevelt opened the meeting that would end the coal strike by apologising for not standing up.

In the room: John Mitchell of the United Mine Workers and three of his district officers; six anthracite operators, led by George F. Baer; Attorney General Knox; Commissioner of Labor Carroll Wright; and the President's secretary. The miners had been out since May and there was no coal.

Roosevelt read a short statement. This is the sentence that matters:

"I wish to call your attention to the fact that there are three parties affected by the situation in the anthracite trade—the operators, the miners, and the general public. I speak for neither the operators nor the miners, but for the general public."

Mitchell answered first. He wanted to deal with the operators directly, and offered arbitration only as the fallback: "…and if we cannot adjust them that way, Mr. President, we are willing that you shall name a tribunal who shall determine the issues that have resulted in this strike."

The operators refused. Baer lectured the President on the Constitution and finished: "Free government is a contemptible failure if it can only protect the lives and property, and secure the comfort of the people, by compromising with the violators of the law and the instigators of violence and crime." Behind the bluster he had an argument: anthracite was losing ground to cheaper soft coal, and a ten per cent rise in wages genuinely threatened the margin. The independent operator John Markle asked, "Are you asking us to deal with a set of outlaws?"

Writing to Governor Crane nineteen days later, Roosevelt said that but for the office he held he would have taken one of the operators "by the seat of the breeches and the nape of the neck and chucked him out of that window." Biographers differ over which one he meant.

He was not soft on the other side. With the operators gone he told Mitchell that if the violence in the coal regions continued he would stop it himself, within twenty-four hours.

The bells struck five. Mitchell told the reporters there had been no settlement. That night Roosevelt wrote to Mark Hanna: "Well, I have tried and failed."

The failure did not hold. Thirteen days later he named a commission; a union convention voted to go back, and the men were underground again on the 23rd. The commission ruled the following March: a ten per cent raise, the ten-hour day cut to nine for the men paid by the hour — and a ten per cent rise in the price of coal for the operators. The miners did not win recognition of their union.

#OTD in 1913, Theodore Roosevelt sailed for South America. He was not going to the River of Doubt. Nobody had suggested it yet.

He reached Pier 8 in Brooklyn at twenty to twelve and climbed the steep gangplank of the SS Vandyck, catching at the rope rails as he went: "This is where I commence my mountaineering." Edith was with him, and his cousin Margaret. The naturalist George Cherrie made it aboard at a run after the last gong — he had gone shopping in Manhattan and misjudged the time.

He had lost the election of 1912 eleven months before. He told the reporters who crowded into a room off his cabin that he was going to get into "fighting trim" for the congressional elections of 1914. The night before, at a Progressive farewell dinner, he had promised: "Next spring I shall return to devote myself with whatever strength I have to working with you for the success of the Progressive Party and of the great principles for which the Progressive Party stands."

The itinerary in his pocket that day belonged to Father John Zahm, and it was tame — the Paraná, the Paraguay, the Tapajós, the Negro, the Orinoco. Five of the best-known rivers on the continent, every one of them on the maps. Attached to it were paid lectures in Argentina, Brazil and Chile — the first invitation had come from the Museo Social Argentino — and a collecting expedition for the American Museum of Natural History. A well-financed speaking tour with a scientific tail.

It changed in Rio. On about the 21st of October, Brazil's foreign minister, Lauro Müller, asked him a question: "Colonel Roosevelt, why don't you go down an unknown river?"

Roosevelt's answer: "I want to be the first to go down the unknown river."

It was Colonel Cândido Rondon who put the river on the table, as one of several possible routes. He had come across it five years earlier on a telegraph survey and had not been able to follow it, and he had named it the Rio da Dúvida — the River of Doubt.

What followed was a joint undertaking, Brazilian and American, and it was called that: the Expedição Scientifica Roosevelt-Rondon. Rondon reached the river first — and the Cinta Larga and the Nhambiquara had lived along it long before either colonel saw it.

Written at sea, to his daughter Ethel: "If we have reasonably good luck we shall accomplish something worth accomplishing. But of course there is enough chance in it to make me reluctant to prophesy."

#OTD in 1903, a grand jury in Washington indicted the man who until that April had been the government's own lawyer for the Post Office Department.

James Noble Tyner was seventy-seven and stricken with paralysis — Postmaster General for the last eight months of the Grant administration, and from 1897 Assistant Attorney General for the Post Office Department, appointed by McKinley and kept on by Roosevelt until Postmaster General Payne forced him out in April. On the afternoon of 5 October the District grand jury handed up thirteen indictments. One was his. Because of his condition the usual arrest was dispensed with; he gave bail at his own house.

The New-York Tribune the next morning: "The climax of the postal scandal came to-day, when James Noble Tyner, who for thirty-nine years has been prominent in the service of the government and was formerly Postmaster General of the United States, was indicted by the grand jury for conspiracy to defraud the government he had served so long."

The charge was specific. Tyner's office decided which mail-fraud concerns were shut out of the mails. He and his nephew Harrison J. Barrett, who had been an attorney in that office, were charged with conspiring to keep the mails open to some eighty get-rich-quick bond concerns so that Barrett could take them on as clients in private practice. Barrett was separately charged with agreeing to take fees in cases still pending before him.

Roosevelt had chosen the investigator himself, and he wrote down exactly how:

"I came to the conclusion that the right man to carry on the investigation was the then Fourth Assistant Postmaster-General… Joseph L. Bristow… he said that he did not wish to go into it unless he could be assured that I would stand personally behind him, and, no matter where his inquiries led him, would support him and prevent interference with him. I answered that I would certainly do so."

He also wrote down the pressure. "Several Senators came to me… and said that they were glad I was putting a stop to corruption, but they hoped I would avoid all scandal; that if I would make an example of some one man and then let the others quietly resign, it would avoid a disturbance which might hurt the party."

He did not. "A favorite war-cry in American political life has always been, 'Turn the rascals out.' We made it evident that, as far as we were concerned, this war-cry was pointless; for we turned our own rascals out."

Not all of them. In the same passage he concedes it: "There were two or three other acquittals, of prominent outsiders."

Tyner was one. That April, months before the indictment, his wife had come to his office at closing time with a safe company's man and a second woman of the family, and emptied the safe; the papers went to the Tyner house by messenger. He was acquitted for want of evidence, and died in December 1904.
