On the afternoon of 5 October the District grand jury handed up thirteen indictments. One was his. Because of his condition the usual arrest was dispensed with; he gave bail at his own house.

The New-York Tribune the next morning: "The climax of the postal scandal came to-day, when James Noble Tyner, who for thirty-nine years has been prominent in the service of the government and was formerly Postmaster General of the United States, was indicted by the grand jury for conspiracy to defraud the government he had served so long."

The charge was specific. Tyner's office decided which mail-fraud concerns were shut out of the mails. He and his nephew Harrison J. Barrett, who had been an attorney in that office, were charged with conspiring to keep the mails open to some eighty get-rich-quick bond concerns so that Barrett could take them on as clients in private practice. Barrett was separately charged with agreeing to take fees in cases still pending before him.

Roosevelt had chosen the investigator himself, and he wrote down exactly how:

"I came to the conclusion that the right man to carry on the investigation was the then Fourth Assistant Postmaster-General… Joseph L. Bristow… he said that he did not wish to go into it unless he could be assured that I would stand personally behind him, and, no matter where his inquiries led him, would support him and prevent interference with him. I answered that I would certainly do so."

He also wrote down the pressure. "Several Senators came to me… and said that they were glad I was putting a stop to corruption, but they hoped I would avoid all scandal; that if I would make an example of some one man and then let the others quietly resign, it would avoid a disturbance which might hurt the party."

He did not. "A favorite war-cry in American political life has always been, 'Turn the rascals out.' We made it evident that, as far as we were concerned, this war-cry was pointless; for we turned our own rascals out."

Not all of them. In the same passage he concedes it: "There were two or three other acquittals, of prominent outsiders."

Tyner was one. That April, months before the indictment, his wife had come to his office at closing time with a safe company's man and a second woman of the family, and emptied the safe; the papers went to the Tyner house by messenger. He was acquitted for want of evidence, and died in December 1904.

#OTD in 1880, a twenty-one-year-old wrote in his diary that he had started law school, that he had spent about $2,500 on jewelry, and that he was getting married in three weeks.

The page survives in his own hand. This is what it says, exactly:

"Entered the Columbia Law School; I shall be there every day about six hours, from nine till half-past three. Am having a lovely time at Aunt Annie's but miss Alice dreadfully. I am going to give her a diamond crescent a ruby bracelet and a saphire ring — in all about 2500 dollars! I have been spending money like water for these last two years, but shall economise after I am married. Three weeks from today we are married! I hardly dare believe it; it is too good. Oh my darling, my darling!"

No commas in the list of jewelry. "Saphire" is his spelling, and so is "economise."

Alice Hathaway Lee was nineteen, at her family's house in Chestnut Hill, Massachusetts. He had met her almost exactly two years earlier. "Aunt Annie" was Anna Bulloch Gracie, his mother's sister. Two days earlier he had written that he was staying with "dear Aunt Annie & Uncle Jimmie; in their cosy little house."

The money is worth sitting with. Average annual earnings for a manufacturing worker in 1880 ran about $345, so the three pieces came to something like seven years of a working man's wages. His own cash account for that year records $7,992.50 spent — up from $5,206.59 the year before.

He noticed, which is the interesting part. The sentence about spending money like water is his, about himself, unprompted, in a book nobody else was going to read.

Three weeks from 6 October was the 27th — his own twenty-second birthday. They married that day at the First Parish Church in Brookline.

He never finished the degree. He was drifting from it well before he was elected to the New York State Assembly in 1881, and left Columbia for good in 1882. Thirty-three years later he explained why the teaching had not taken: "The caveat emptor side of the law, like the caveat emptor side of business, seemed to me repellent; it did not make for social fair dealing." And, a few lines on: "I was young; there was much in the judgment which I then formed on this matter which I should now revise."

#OTD in 1901, three weeks into the presidency, Theodore Roosevelt wrote a letter about his dead father on Executive Mansion stationery — and called the building the White House twice.

Sarah Bancroft Leavitt had known his parents. She wrote to him when he took office, and this is what he wrote back:

"I knew I should hear from you, and I loved your letter. Yes, I have thought of father all the time, and of how pleased he would be; what would I not give if only he could have lived until now and seen me here in the White House, and all his grandchildren, and everything! Edith is too sweet and pretty and dignified and wise as mistress of the White House, and very happy with it; she will write you soon.

Do you know that at the end of my term here, in 1905, I shall be exactly the age father was when he died?

Unconsciously, I always find I am trying to model myself with my children on the way he was with us."

He signed it "Lovingly yours."

Two things about that letter.

The first is the letterhead. It reads EXECUTIVE MANSION, WASHINGTON — and he writes "the White House" twice in the body, a name that had been turning up in print for most of the century, though most people still said Executive Mansion. Ten days later his secretary wrote to the Secretary of State directing that official papers carry the White House dateline from then on. He did not invent the name. He made it official.

The second is the arithmetic, and he had it slightly wrong. Theodore Roosevelt Sr. died on 9 February 1878, aged forty-six years and four months. On the day his son's term would have ended, in March 1905, he would have been thirteen days short of that. And it never happened anyway — he ran in 1904, won, and left the office in 1909 at fifty.

Mrs. Leavitt had known his father through the New York Orthopaedic Dispensary, which Theodore Sr. helped found. In February 1916 Roosevelt wrote to her again: "Of course if I spoke at all I had to speak of you and Father and Aunt Annie; you are always associated with them, and with my dear, charming mother, in my mind."

He wrote that one on the ninth of February.

#OTD in 1909, in camp beside a river in British East Africa, Theodore Roosevelt's diary entry for the whole day was one word.

Wrote.

That is the entire page. The printed columns for weather and temperature are blank. Nothing else.

Turn back one leaf and Thursday looks like this: "2 gazelle, 100 yards / 1 oryx, 120 / 1 giraffe, cow, 130" — and then, taking up the rest of the page, a giraffe he drew himself in the same purple pencil, with a couple of antelope heads sketched underneath it.

He was not being cryptic. He kept this diary like a ledger, and he did it often — "Wrote" turns up alone twice in 1909, and "Writing" and "Blank" stand alone too, along with a run of bare place names: Naples, Messina, Aden, Entebbe.

What he was writing was the reason the trip could happen at all. Scribner's had paid him $50,000 for the magazine rights to twelve articles, with the book a separate arrangement. The month he spent in that camp became the chapter on the Guaso Nyero, published in Scribner's Magazine the following July.

He had been in Africa five and a half months. Kermit had gone off to the southwest on 21 September, and the only other European in camp was the professional hunter R. J. Cuninghame. The men who made the camp work were African, and Roosevelt named them: "my four regular attendants, Bakhari and Gouvimali the gun-bearers, Simba the sais, and Kiboko the skinner." Simba is the one to remember. Earlier in the trip, on the Kapiti Plains, a lion turned and came at them; Simba ran up on foot and took the bridle, and Roosevelt would not ride off and leave him. "Good, Simba," he said, "now we'll see this thing through" — and shot the lion with his elbow resting on Simba's shoulder. Of the name, he wrote: "Simba, a lion, and as I shall later show he was not unworthy of it."

It was a collecting expedition for the Smithsonian, and it killed a great deal. By Roosevelt's own tally at the back of African Game Trails he shot 296 animals and Kermit 216. The expedition as a whole killed or trapped some 11,400 — most of them small mammals, birds and reptiles taken by the naturalists.

On this particular day he shot nothing and went nowhere.

#OTD in 1899, a man named S. R. Wharton wrote to the governor of New York proposing to launch him at the presidency. The governor forwarded the letter to a friend with one sentence of verdict.

"I send you the enclosed from S. R. Wharton. It seems to me that such a movement as he suggests would be altogether premature and ill-advised."

Premature is the word to notice. Wharton's letter does not survive, but Elting Morison, who edited Roosevelt's correspondence, judged he was proposing a campaign for 1904 — five years out. Roosevelt had been governor for nine months; eighteen months before that he had been a lieutenant colonel of volunteers. That July he had told Lodge he was not a candidate for the War Department and could not leave Albany. What he wanted next was a second term as governor.

And the letter does not stop there. The second paragraph is the good part:

"The President, when I was at the Dewey dinner at the White House, insisted upon my going to Cincinnati — I mean literally insisted, and would not take no for an answer, so I had to reluctantly accede. He then did his best to get me to go to Nebraska and Iowa, but here I finally refused, for I agree with you that if I went at all I would find it very difficult not to go everywhere."

So: batting away a presidential boom in one sentence, and in the next being hauled around the country by the sitting President.

The friend was Herman Kohlsaat, who owned two Chicago papers, had helped bail McKinley out of a ruinous debt in 1893, and four years before this had sponsored what is usually called America's first automobile race. He was the one telling Roosevelt to stay off the road.

Sixteen days later, to Lodge, from the Union League Club in New York:

"After sending you that Oregon letter yesterday I suddenly thought you might regard it as a sympton of desire on my part to get into the Presidential campaign. Heaven forbid! I wrote the writer at once that of course McKinley was inevitable, and that I was not in the race in any way or shape."

"Sympton" is his spelling.

#OTD in 1910, a former president climbed into an open biplane at a field outside St. Louis, sat down on the wing beside the pilot, and went up. No cockpit. No belt.

He had not planned it. He was on a campaign swing for the Missouri Republicans, and the aviator — Arch Hoxsey of the Wright exhibition team — had set an American distance record three days earlier, flying 104 miles from Springfield, Illinois. By Hoxsey's own account in the New-York Tribune the next morning, he made the offer and Roosevelt took about a second over it.

"Here's your chance."

"All right; let's not make too much fuss about it while I am getting into the machine."

Then two laps of Kinloch Field — about three miles, at something like a hundred feet, in three minutes and twenty seconds. Partway round he caught sight of the grandstand and waved at it, which made the machine wobble.

On the ground he turned to the pilot: "Hoxsey, you're all right!"

To the reporters: "It was great! First class!… I wish I could stay up for an hour, but I haven't the time this afternoon."

And that evening, at the governor's dinner: "That was the bulliest experience I ever had. I envy you, your professional conquest of space."

He was the first American president ever to leave the ground — but the word order matters. He was a *former* president, nineteen months out of office. No sitting president would fly for another thirty-two years, when Franklin Roosevelt crossed the Atlantic to Casablanca in January 1943.

Not quite seven years had passed since Kitty Hawk.

Someone was filming, and the reel survives at the Library of Congress: a fifty-one-year-old ex-president in a cloth cap, being handed up into a machine made of spruce, wire and muslin.

Arch Hoxsey was in his twenties. Eighty-one days later, on the last day of that year, he took a Wright biplane up over Dominguez Field in Los Angeles to beat his own altitude record of 11,474 feet. He was killed in the fall.

#OTD in 1912, a weekly newspaper in Ishpeming, Michigan, printed one sentence about Theodore Roosevelt. Seven months later it cost its publisher six cents and the central charge he had made.

Iron Ore, Saturday, October 12, 1912, under the heading "The Roosevelt Way":

"Roosevelt lies and curses in a most disgusting way; he gets drunk, too, and that not infrequently, and all his intimates know about it."

Most of the editorial is about the other charge — that he called everyone else a liar and could not take it back. It ends: "For so great a fighter, self-styled, he is the poorest loser we ever knew."

Roosevelt sued. He was in Mercy Hospital in Chicago when the papers were filed, with a bullet in his chest from Milwaukee two days after the editorial ran.

The trial opened at Marquette in May 1913. He brought his witnesses north on a train — Jacob Riis, his physicians, three men who had sat in his cabinet — and read in the depositions of a dozen more.

"I have never been drunk or in the slightest degree under the influence of liquor."

"I have never drunk a high-ball or cocktail in my life. I have sometimes drunk mint juleps in the White House. There was a bed of mint there, and I may have drunk half a dozen mint juleps a year, and certainly no more."

On May 31 the publisher, George A. Newett, read a statement. He had taken more than forty depositions. He had found people who would swear they had watched Roosevelt speak and believed he was drunk. He had found no one who had seen it.

"It is fair to the plaintiff to state that I have been unable to find in any section of the country any individual witness who is willing to state that he has personally seen Mr. Roosevelt drink to excess… I am forced to the conclusion that I was mistaken."

The suit had asked $10,000. Roosevelt stood and gave it up on the spot.

"Your Honor, in view of the statement of the defendant, I ask the Court to instruct the jury that I desire only nominal damages.

I did not go into this suit for money. I did not go into it for any vindictive purpose. I went into it, and, as the Court has said, I made my reputation an issue, because I wished, once for all during my lifetime, thoroughly and comprehensively to deal with these slanders, so that never again will it be possible for any man, in good faith, to repeat them.

I have achieved my purpose, and I am content."

Nominal damages under Michigan law were six cents. The court found Newett had published in good faith and without malice.

Two things the record is careful about. Newett was a teetotaler, and he had been postmaster of Ishpeming — an appointment, as he said on the stand, "from the plaintiff in this case."

And he took back only the drinking charge. On the other, Riis testified that he had never heard Roosevelt "use any unclean or profane language," only "the expression 'Godfrey' when he gets very much excited."

#OTD in 1902, at about a quarter to ten at night, there was a knock at the President's door. The financier J. Pierpont Morgan had come down from New York, and he had an answer.

The anthracite strike was 154 days old and the country was out of coal. Roosevelt was in temporary quarters on Jackson Place — the White House was being rebuilt — and on crutches. A trolley had run into his carriage in September, killing a Secret Service agent, and a surgeon had scraped his shinbone three weeks later.

What the winter looked like, from the New-York Tribune: on the East Side, people filling coal pails at fifteen cents apiece — at least fifty thousand of them in a day.

Ten days earlier he had brought the operators and the miners' president into that parlour and failed. What he did next he told plainly years later. He sent for Major-General John M. Schofield.

"I sent for him, telling him that if I had to make use of him it would be because the crisis was only less serious than that of the Civil War, that the action taken would be practically a war measure, and that if I sent him he must act in a purely military capacity under me as commander-in-chief, paying no heed to any authority, judicial or otherwise, except mine."

The orders, if they came, were to dispossess the operators and run the mines. They never came.

On the 11th, Secretary of War Elihu Root went to New York and spent most of a day with Morgan aboard his yacht, the Corsair. Root's account, in a letter to Roosevelt the following June: "we drafted an agreement of arbitration for a commission to be appointed by you."

Two days later Morgan came to Washington with Robert Bacon, reached the Arlington at half past nine, and fifteen minutes later walked over with Root, carrying the operators' answer. The conference ran to ten minutes to twelve. Morgan left and said nothing to reporters.

The operators would take a commission — but one built of five named categories, none of them a labour man. Two nights later he broke that by appointing the head of a railway union and calling him the "eminent sociologist." He never got over it:

"I shall never forget the mixture of relief and amusement I felt when I thoroughly grasped the fact that while they would heroically submit to anarchy rather than have Tweedledum, yet if I would call it Tweedledee they would accept it with rapture… In order to carry the great and vital point and secure agreement by both parties, all that was necessary for me to do was to commit a technical and nominal absurdity with a solemn face. This I gladly did."

The names went out at twenty past two in the morning on the 16th; the miners went back on the 23rd. The award came the following March: a ten per cent raise, a shorter day, and no recognition of the union.

#OTD in 1886, a twenty-seven-year-old was nominated for mayor of New York without being in the room. He found out from a reporter.

The Republican county convention met at the Grand Opera House and named him by acclamation. Theodore Roosevelt was across town at the Union League Club when a man from the Tribune brought him the news.

"It comes to me somewhat in the nature of a surprise, for, until eight o'clock last evening, I had not been spoken to formally on the subject of the nomination for the Mayoralty. While very reluctant to accept it, the matter has been presented to me in such a light as to make me feel it impossible to refuse."

On what the job would take, he was less careful: the man who held it "must be willing and able to use the knife with merciless thoroughness in cutting out the countless already long-existing abuses."

Consider where he was standing. Two years and eight months earlier, his wife and his mother had died in the same house on the same day. He had gone to the Dakota Badlands. He came back east that autumn with a book written and a ranch behind him, and the party handed him a race it did not expect him to win.

It did not. On 2 November the count was Abram Hewitt 90,552, Henry George 68,110, Theodore Roosevelt 60,435. Third, in his own city — and by then he was twenty-eight, the formal ratification having been at Cooper Union on the 27th, his birthday.

And then he did something nobody in that convention hall knew about.

For eleven months he had been secretly engaged to Edith Kermit Carow, a childhood friend, a fact he had kept from almost everyone because a widower remarrying so soon was a thing people talked about. Four days after losing the election he sailed for England on the Cunard liner Etruria. He had booked passage for himself and his sister Bamie as "Mr. and Miss Merrifield" — the name of his Dakota ranch partner.

On 2 December they were married at St George's, Hanover Square, in a London fog so thick that link-bearers had to guide his carriage to the door and the fog hung inside the nave. He wore orange gloves.

One hundred and twenty-five years ago today, Booker T. Washington became the first African American to dine as a guest of the President and his family at the White House.

Every word of that sentence is doing work. Black Americans had been to the White House before — Sojourner Truth met Lincoln in his office in 1864, Frederick Douglass came to the second inaugural reception in 1865, the soprano Marie Selika Williams sang there in 1878. What had not happened was this: a seat at the family table.

Washington had come into Washington by train from a lecture tour in Mississippi and was staying at the house of Whitefield McKinlay on Eleventh Street. The invitation was waiting when he got there. He wrote about it ten years later:

"When I reached Mr. McKinlay's house I found an invitation from President Roosevelt asking me to dine with him at the White House that evening at eight o'clock."

The note Roosevelt actually sent said half past seven. Eight o'clock is Washington's memory, a decade on.

Roosevelt had been President for a month. At the table were Edith, four of the children — Kermit, Ethel, Archie and Quentin — and one other guest, Philip Stewart of Colorado. Washington and Stewart sat on either side of the President.

It was a working dinner. The two men had been corresponding since Roosevelt's first week in office about federal appointments in the South, and that is what they discussed. Washington's own account of the evening is four sentences long:

"At the hour appointed I went to the White House and dined with the President and members of his family and a gentleman from Colorado. After dinner we talked at considerable length concerning plans about the South which the President had in mind. I left the White House almost immediately and took a train the same night for New York."

No photograph of the dinner exists. Two years later a Chicago company printed the last picture in this post — an invented scene, the two men alone at a small round table, Lincoln's portrait on the wall, the word Equality across the cloth. Its own caption dates the dinner to October 17th, which is the day the story broke, not the day it happened. It is not a record of the evening. It is a record of what some Americans wanted the evening to mean.

What happened next was not planned by anyone. The White House gave reporters its routine list of the day's callers, as it did every day. One line went out on the wires overnight.

Booker T. Washington, of Tuskegee, Ala., dined with the President last evening.

Tomorrow: the country reads it.

#OTD in 1901, the country found out that Booker T. Washington had eaten dinner at the White House, and a great many white Americans lost their minds.

It got out because of paperwork. A reporter working the White House late that night found the name on the day's list of callers. One line moved on the wires and ran in the morning papers.

Booker T. Washington, of Tuskegee, Ala., dined with the President last evening.

The Memphis Scimitar called it "the most damnable outrage which has ever been perpetrated by any citizen of the United States." The Richmond Times said it meant Roosevelt saw no reason "why whites and blacks may not marry and intermarry." The Memphis Commercial Appeal: "this is a white man's country. President Roosevelt has committed a blunder that is worse than a crime."

And a sitting United States senator, Benjamin Tillman of South Carolina, said this out loud:

"The action of President Roosevelt in entertaining that nigger will necessitate our killing a thousand niggers in the South before they will learn their place again."

The scale is measurable. In the fifteen days after the dinner, Washington's name appears on 435 pages of the newspapers digitized in the Library of Congress's Chronicling America — 69 of them in the first four days.

That is the half of this story everybody knows. Here is the half that got buried.

The Washington Bee, a Black paper in the capital, put Washington's portrait on its front page that Saturday under the line "No color line in the White House — An Object Lesson for the South." A week later it asked the obvious question: "Hasn't a man the right to invite whom he pleases to his house?"

The Colored American: "President Roosevelt is the Chief Magistrate of the whole people. As such, it was perfectly natural for him to recognize the most conspicious representative of a race constituting one eighth of the population of the United States." (The spelling is theirs.)

The Cleveland Gazette called the dinner "perfectly right and proper," then printed a warning that reads now like prophecy: it "will eventually prove the latter's undoing, as far as his great educational work is concerned."

And on 22 October, at its annual meeting in Oak Park, Illinois, the American Missionary Association adopted — without a dissenting voice — a resolution of approval for a President "thus ignoring race prejudice."

Washington himself said nothing. He never gave an interview about that evening, and when a paper printed one anyway he answered flatly: "I want to state as emphatically as I can that I have given no interview…" He did not write about it until his 1911 memoir.

Roosevelt, privately, at the end of that month: "I shall have him to dine just as often as I please."

He never did.

#OTD in 1905, four years after the dinner, Theodore Roosevelt boarded a train for the South.

It left Washington at half past eight in the morning. Fredericksburg just after ten. Ashland for three minutes, long enough for the Randolph-Macon College students. Richmond by noon. He spoke in Capitol Square that afternoon, and at the luncheon that followed he said this:

"Next only to a man's having worn the blue comes the fact of the man's having worn the gray, as entitling him to honor in my sight."

Two days later he was at Roswell, Georgia. He walked through the house where his mother grew up, then spoke in the town park.

"It has been my very great good fortune to have the right to claim that my blood is half Southern and half Northern."

He meant it literally. Martha Bulloch was a Georgia girl; her brothers served the Confederacy, and one of them, Irvine, was — Roosevelt told the crowd — the man who fired the last two shots from the raider Alabama before she went down off Cherbourg. He told that story to a Georgia crowd, about his own uncle, as President of the United States.

The tour ran nine days through seven states and ended at New Orleans. The press called it a triumph.

Here is what he did not say, in nine days, in a run of speeches that fills a volume.
